label: Supplementary practice — 1000 MCQ Statistics Test Series (PDF pages 958, 963, 971, 1008, 376)

items.stem: Let A be a symmetric idempotent p×p matrix of rank r
statements: Y′AY and Y′(Iₚ−A)Y are independent chi-square variables, each with 2r degrees of freedom.
items.explanation: A symmetric idempotent matrix is an orthogonal projection. Its rank r gives Y′AY~χ²(r). The complementary projection Iₚ−A has rank p−r, so its quadratic form has χ²(p−r), not χ²(r) in general. The sum is Y′Y~χ²(p), not χ²(2r) in general. The two forms are independent, but their degrees of freedom are r and p−r. Only A is true as written.

A.why: A standard normal quadratic form with a symmetric idempotent matrix of rank r is chi-square with r degrees of freedom.

B.why: The complementary projection has rank p−r.

C.why: The sum is Y′Y, which has chi-square p degrees of freedom.

D.why: The forms are independent, but their degrees of freedom are r and p−r, not both 2r.

items.repaired: The scan marks A, C and D. The mathematical result gives A only as written; the other degrees of freedom are p−r and p.

items.stem: For a bivariate normal pair (X,Y) with standard deviations σ₁,σ₂ and correlation ρ, which pair is independent if and only if σ₁=σ₂?
items.explanation: For jointly normal variables, zero covariance is equivalent to independence. Cov(X+Y,X−Y)=Var(X)−Var(Y)=σ₁²−σ₂² because the cross-covariance terms cancel. This is zero exactly when σ₁=σ₂. Therefore X+Y and X−Y are independent exactly under the stated condition.

A.why: Their covariance is ρσ₁σ₂, which is not zero for every equal-standard-deviation case.

B.why: The covariance is Var(X)−Cov(X,Y), not identically zero when σ₁=σ₂.

C.why: The covariance is Cov(X,Y)+Var(Y), not identically zero when σ₁=σ₂.

D.why: Their covariance is σ₁²−σ₂², and joint normality makes zero covariance equivalent to independence.

items.stem: Let R₁₂.₃ be the sample multiple correlation of X₁ on X₂,X₃, and R₁₂.₃₄ the sample multiple correlation of X₁ on X₂,X₃,X₄. Which pair is possible?
items.explanation: A multiple correlation coefficient is nonnegative. Also, adding a predictor cannot decrease the maximised squared correlation: the larger regression model can always set the new coefficient to zero and reproduce the smaller model. Thus R₁₂.₃₄≥R₁₂.₃. Only the pair 0.3 followed by 0.7 satisfies both properties.

items.stem: Let Y~N₃(μ,Σ), where μ=(2,−3,1)′ and Σ=[[1,1,1],[1,3,2],[1,2,2]]. Find the distribution of 3X₁−2X₂+X₃.
items.explanation: A linear combination a′Y of a multivariate normal vector is normal with mean a′μ and variance a′Σa. Here a=(3,−2,1)′. The mean is 3(2)−2(−3)+1=13. Multiplying Σa gives (2,−1,1)′, so a′Σa=3(2)+(−2)(−1)+1=9. The distribution is N(13,9).

items.stem: If px+qy+r=0 is the regression line of Y on X and qx+py+s=0 is the regression line of X on Y, which relation must hold?
items.explanation: From the first line, Y=−(p/q)X−r/q, so the regression coefficient of Y on X is bᵧₓ=−p/q. From the second line, X=−(p/q)Y−s/q, so the regression coefficient of X on Y is bₓᵧ=−p/q. The product of the two regression coefficients equals the squared correlation, rₓᵧ², which cannot exceed one. Thus p²/q²≤1, giving p²≤q². Option A is correct.

items.stem: X₁, X₂ and X₃ are independent random variables with variances 1, 4 and 9, respectively. Find the correlation coefficient between Y=X₁−X₂ and Z=X₂+X₃.
items.explanation: Because X₁,X₂,X₃ are independent, Cov(X₁,X₂)=Cov(X₁,X₃)=Cov(X₂,X₃)=0. Hence Cov(Y,Z)=Cov(X₁−X₂,X₂+X₃)=−Var(X₂)=−4. Also Var(Y)=Var(X₁)+Var(X₂)=1+4=5 and Var(Z)=Var(X₂)+Var(X₃)=4+9=13. Therefore Corr(Y,Z)=−4/√(5×13)=−4/(√5√13), option C.

items.stem: Let (X,Y) have a bivariate standard normal distribution with correlation ρ, and let p=P(XY>0). Express ρ in terms of p.
items.explanation: For a standard bivariate normal pair, P(XY>0)=1/2+(1/π)arcsin(ρ). Therefore p−1/2=arcsin(ρ)/π, so ρ=sin(π(p−1/2)). Using sin(a−π/2)=−cos(a), this equals −cos(πp). Since cos(π(1−p))=−cos(πp), we obtain ρ=cos(π(1−p)). This is option A with q=1−p.

items.stem: Let X₁ and X₂ be independent Poisson random variables with means μ₁ and μ₂. Find the regression coefficient of X₁ on X₁+X₂.
items.explanation: The regression coefficient of X₁ on S=X₁+X₂ is Cov(X₁,S)/Var(S). Since X₁ and X₂ are independent, Cov(X₁,S)=Cov(X₁,X₁)+Cov(X₁,X₂)=Var(X₁)=μ₁. Also Var(S)=Var(X₁)+Var(X₂)=μ₁+μ₂. Therefore the coefficient is μ₁/(μ₁+μ₂), option A.

items.stem: Let X and Y be iid N(0,1). Which statement is NOT true?
options: Y/X and X/Y are identically distributed.
(X,X+Y) is bivariate normal with variances 1 and 2 and correlation 1/√2.
items.explanation: Because X and Y are iid continuous variables, P(X<Y)=1/2. The ratio Y/X has a standard Cauchy distribution, so P(Y/X<1)=1/2+arctan(1)/π=3/4. These probabilities are not equal, so B is false. A follows because Cov(X+Y,X−Y)=Var(X)−Var(Y)=0 and the pair is jointly normal. C is true because both a standard Cauchy variable and its reciprocal have the same distribution. D is true because the vector is a linear transformation of a jointly normal vector, with variances 1 and 2 and covariance 1.

items.stem: Let X₁,X₂,X₃ be iid N(0,1). Find the dispersion (covariance) matrix of (X₁, X₁+X₂, X₁+X₂+X₃)ᵀ.
items.explanation: Let Y₁=X₁, Y₂=X₁+X₂ and Y₃=X₁+X₂+X₃. Since the Xi are independent with variance one, Var(Y₁)=1, Var(Y₂)=2 and Var(Y₃)=3. Cov(Y₁,Y₂)=Var(X₁)=1; Cov(Y₁,Y₃)=1; and Cov(Y₂,Y₃)=Var(X₁)+Var(X₂)=2. Filling the symmetric covariance matrix gives [[1,1,1],[1,2,2],[1,2,3]], option C.

items.stem: Let S=Σᵢ₌₁³⁰ xᵢxᵢᵀ, where each xᵢ is a column vector with 29 components. What is the attainable maximum rank of S?
items.explanation: Each outer product xᵢxᵢᵀ is a 29×29 matrix, so S is also 29×29 and its rank cannot exceed 29. With 30 vectors in 29-dimensional space, they can span the full 29-dimensional space, making rank 29 attainable. Therefore the maximum rank is 29, option B.

items.stem: Which of the following matrices is a valid correlation matrix?
items.explanation: A correlation matrix must be symmetric, have ones on the diagonal, and be positive semidefinite. Matrix A has diagonal entries 0.5 rather than 1 and is not positive semidefinite. Matrix B is not symmetric. Matrix D is not symmetric. Matrix C is the 2×2 identity matrix, which satisfies all requirements. Therefore C is valid.

items.stem: Let (X₁,X₂) have a bivariate normal distribution with E(X₁)=E(X₂)=0, Var(X₁)=Var(X₂)=1 and Cov(X₁,X₂)=1/2. Find P(X₁+2X₂>√7).
items.explanation: A linear combination of jointly normal variables is normal. Its mean is zero and variance is Var(X₁)+4Var(X₂)+4Cov(X₁,X₂)=1+4+2=7. Therefore (X₁+2X₂)/√7 is standard normal, and the required probability is P(Z>1)=0.1587.

items.stem: Let (X,Y) have joint density f(x,y)=1/4(1+xy) for |x|<1 and |y|<1, and zero elsewhere. Which statement is correct?
options: X and Y are independent and identically distributed.
X and Y are independent but not identically distributed.
X and Y are identically distributed but not independent.
items.explanation: Find the marginal density of X by integrating over y: f_X(x)=∫₋₁¹(1/4)(1+xy)dy=1/2 for −1<x<1, because the integral of y over the symmetric interval is zero. Similarly f_Y(y)=1/2 for −1<y<1. Thus X and Y have the same Uniform(−1,1) distribution. If they were independent, the joint density would equal f_X(x)f_Y(y)=1/4, but the given joint density is (1+xy)/4, which varies with x and y. They are identically distributed but dependent.

items.stem: Which of the following matrices can be the variance-covariance matrix of a two-dimensional random vector?
items.explanation: A covariance matrix must be symmetric and positive semidefinite. Option A is symmetric, has positive diagonal entries, and determinant 2·1−(−1)²=1>0, so it is positive definite and valid. Option B is not symmetric. Option C has a negative diagonal entry, which would mean a negative variance. Option D is symmetric but has determinant 1·2−2²=−2<0, so it is not positive semidefinite. Only A can be a covariance matrix.
